hints: Think about what acidity means in water, loss of $\text{H}^{+}$ from the $\text{O-H}$ group to leave a negative ion, and which negative ion is most stable.
Compare what is attached to the $\text{O-H}$ group in each case, a $\text{C=O}$ group, a benzene ring directly, or an alkyl group.
Recall how withdrawing electrons from $\text{O-H}$ weakens it, while pushing electrons toward $\text{O-H}$ strengthens it and destabilises the anion.
walkthrough:
Picture acidity as losing a proton**
Imagine each molecule as $\text{RO-H}$ breaking to $\text{RO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+}$. The easier that $\text{O-H}$ bond breaks, and the more stable the $\text{RO}^{-}$ left behind, the stronger the acid. So you are really comparing $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COO}^{-}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$.

Place benzoic acid at the top**
In $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$ the $\text{OH}$ is joined to $\text{C=O}$. Oxygen in $\text{C=O}$ is very electronegative, so the $\text{COOH}$ group pulls electrons toward itself. That is the negative inductive, electron withdrawing effect. It pulls electron density away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond, weakening it, so $\text{H}^{+}$ leaves easily. The resulting carboxylate anion is also stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge over two oxygens.

Place phenol in the middle**
In $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ the O is joined directly to the benzene ring. One of the lone pairs on O sits in a p-orbital that overlaps with the ring $\pi$-system, so it is delocalised into the ring. That withdrawal of electron density also weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and helps stabilise the phenoxide ion, but the effect is smaller than the strong $\text{C=O}$ withdrawal plus the extra resonance stabilisation in a carboxylate. So phenol is weaker than benzoic acid.

Place ethanol at the bottom**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ the O is joined to an ethyl group. Alkyl groups push electrons away, the positive inductive, electron donating effect. That pushes extra electron density onto O, strengthening the $\text{O-H}$ bond so $\text{H}^{+}$ is held more tightly, and it intensifies the negative charge on $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$, destabilising it. So ethanol is the least acidic.

Final answer: most acidic benzoic acid > phenol > ethanol least acidic.
Benzoic acid is strongest as the $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$ group has a negative inductive, electron withdrawing effect which weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond so $\text{H}^{+}$ is lost more easily and stabilises the carboxylate anion.
Phenol is intermediate as the lone pair on O overlaps / is delocalised into the benzene $\pi$-system, weakening the $\text{O-H}$ bond.
Ethanol is weakest as the ethyl group has a positive inductive, electron donating effect which strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and destabilises the ethoxide anion.

hints: Recall that $\text{COOH}$ deactivates the ring and directs to the meta position, while $\text{OH}$ strongly activates and directs to ortho and para positions.
Use the given molecular formulae $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{4}$ and $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{3}$ to confirm monosubstitution by one $\text{NO}_{2}$ group in each case.
walkthrough:
Let the existing group steer the new group**
In nitration the electrophile $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ attacks the ring. The group already on the ring controls where it goes. $\text{COOH}$ is electron withdrawing and deactivating, so it directs meta. $\text{OH}$ is electron donating by lone pair delocalisation and strongly activating, so it directs ortho and para.

Draw the two isomers**
For benzoic acid, put $\text{NO}_{2}$ meta to $\text{COOH}$ to give 3-nitrobenzoic acid. That matches $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{4}$. For phenol, put $\text{NO}_{2}$ ortho to $\text{OH}$ to give 2-nitrophenol. That matches $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{3}$. Draw each as a hexagon with the two substituents in the correct relative positions.

Final answer: Major product from benzoic acid: 3-nitrobenzoic acid, benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NO}_{2}$ in meta / 3-positions to each other.
Major product from phenol: 2-nitrophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_{2}$ in ortho / 2-positions to each other.

hints: Split the ester $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ into the acid part and the alcohol part to name alkyl alkanoate.
walkthrough:
Name as alkyl alkanoate**
Look at Fig. 7.2: left side $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)-}$ comes from propanoic acid, so propanoate. Right side $\text{-OCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ comes from ethanol, so ethyl. Combine to give ethyl propanoate, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOC}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$.

hints: Identify the electrophile as the carbonyl C in $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(=O)Cl}$ and the nucleophile as a lone pair on O in $\text{R-O-H}$.
Remember to show the $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$ dipole and the curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O when the nucleophile attacks.
Think about what the central C is bonded to after addition, with both Cl and $\text{O}^{+}\text{HR}$ present plus two O atoms.
Consider how the $\text{C=O}$ reforms by expelling $\text{Cl}^{-}$, using an arrow from $\text{O}^{-}$ back to $\text{C-O}$ and an arrow from $\text{C-Cl}$ to Cl.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrophile and nucleophile**
The carbonyl C in $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}-\text{C(=O)-Cl}$ is $\delta+$ because O is more electronegative, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Ethanol $\text{R-O-H}$ has two lone pairs on O. One of those lone pairs is the nucleophile that will attack the $\delta+$ C.

Show the addition step**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on O in $\text{R-O-H}$ to the carbonyl C, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond to the O. This breaks the $\pi$-bond to give $\text{O}^{-}$ and forms a new $\text{C-O}^{+}\text{HR}$ bond. The central C is now tetrahedral, bonded to $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}$, $\text{O}^{-}$, $\text{O}^{+}\text{HR}$ and Cl. That is your organic intermediate box.

Show the elimination step**
Now reform the $\text{C=O}$. Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair / negative charge on $\text{O}^{-}$ back to form the $\text{C-O}$ double bond, and a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to Cl to expel $\text{Cl}^{-}$. This collapses the tetrahedron to $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOR}$ plus HCl after deprotonation.

Check the formal details**
Make sure every O has correct lone pairs, every arrow starts at a lone pair or bond and ends at an atom or bond, all $+$ and $-$ charges are shown, and the $\text{C=O}$ dipole is labelled. That precision earns the mechanism marks.

Final answer: Attack of lone pair on O of $\text{R-O-H}$ on $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C=O}^{\delta-}$ in $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$ with $\text{C=O}$ arrow to O to give tetrahedral intermediate $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}-\text{C}(\text{O}^{-})(\text{O}^{+}\text{HR})(\text{Cl})$; then $\text{O}^{-}$ reforms $\text{C=O}$ expelling $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to give ester + HCl. Full lone pairs, dipoles, curly arrows, charges and intermediate shown.

hints: Recall the two stage name for acyl chloride reactions where the nucleophile first adds to $\text{C=O}$ then $\text{Cl}^{-}$ leaves.
walkthrough:
Link the two stages to the name**
You just drew addition of $\text{R-OH}$ to the $\text{C=O}$ to make a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by elimination of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to reform $\text{C=O}$. That two word sequence is nucleophilic addition-elimination.
